title: Screening & mechanism design
text: Screening (principal–agent with adverse selection) studies how a principal designs a menu of contracts to induce agents to reveal private information. Mechanism design generalizes this: choose rules to implement outcomes given strategic agents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text: Screening (principal–agent with adverse selection) studies how a principal designs a menu of contracts to induce agents to reveal private information. Mechanism design generalizes this: choose rules to implement outcomes given strategic agents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
What’s special

Key constraint: incentive compatibility (each type prefers its intended option).
Participation (individual rationality) often binds for the lowest type.
Design trades off efficiency vs information rents.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
One example (two-type contract menu)
Agent type \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) (productivity). Principal offers contracts \((w,q)\): wage and required output.
Utility: \(u = w - c(q,\theta)\), where \(c(q,H) < c(q,L)\) (high type has lower cost).
Principal wants higher \(q\) from \(H\) but must prevent \(H\) from pretending to be \(L\).
Solution sketch. The optimal menu typically: - distorts the low-type contract downward (lower \(q\)) to reduce information rents, - gives the high type a contract with higher \(q\) and positive rent, - satisfies IC constraints: \(H\) prefers \(H\)-contract; \(L\) prefers \(L\)-contract.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Story
An insurer can’t observe customer risk. It offers two plans (a menu). Customers self-select. The insurer designs the menu so each type reveals itself by choosing the plan intended for it.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Model

Types \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) privately known
Contracts \((p,q)\): premium \(p\) and coverage \(q\)
Utility: \(u_\theta(p,q)=v_\theta(q)-p\)
Goal: maximize profit subject to incentive constraints

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Equilibrium constraints (IC/IR)
Incentive compatibility: \[
u_H(p_H,q_H)\ge u_H(p_L,q_L),
\qquad
u_L(p_L,q_L)\ge u_L(p_H,q_H).
\]
Individual rationality: \[
u_\theta(p_\theta,q_\theta)\ge 0 \quad (\theta\in\{H,L\}).
\]

title: Screening & mechanism design
section: What the solution typically looks like (high-level)
text:
What the solution typically looks like (high-level)

Low-type contract is often distorted (less generous) to reduce information rents.
High type receives more generous terms and may earn positive information rent.

title: Screening & mechanism design
text:
Later-on analysis

Moral hazard: if effort is hidden too, the design problem changes (adverse selection + moral hazard).
Multiple dimensions: risk + risk aversion produces richer menus.
Mechanism design view: “contract menus” are a specific mechanism; the general theory asks what outcomes are implementable.

title: Cheap talk
text: Cheap talk is communication that is costless and non-binding: a sender sends a message, then a receiver chooses an action.

title: Cheap talk
text: Cheap talk is communication that is costless and non-binding: a sender sends a message, then a receiver chooses an action.

title: Cheap talk
text:
What’s special

Messages have no direct payoff effect, so credibility comes only from aligned incentives.
Information can still be partially transmitted when preferences are not too misaligned.
Outcomes typically depend on how strongly the sender wants to bias the receiver’s action.

title: Cheap talk
text:
One example

Setup (a stylized version)

State: \(\theta \in [0,1]\) is known to the sender.
Message: \(m\) is any costless statement.
Receiver chooses action \(a\in[0,1]\).

Payoffs: - Receiver wants \(a\) close to \(\theta\). - Sender wants \(a\) close to \(\theta + b\) (bias \(b>0\)).


Key idea
If the bias \(b\) is small, the sender can truthfully separate states into intervals (“coarse truth”), and the receiver best-responds by choosing the expected state within the reported interval. If \(b\) is large, communication becomes uninformative (pooling).

title: Cheap talk
text:
Story
You ask a friend for a restaurant recommendation in a new city. Your friend knows the options. But your tastes differ: they love loud, spicy places; you want calm and mild. They aren’t lying—they just have a bias.
Cheap talk studies whether costless messages can still transmit information when incentives aren’t perfectly aligned.

title: Cheap talk
text:
Model

State \(\theta\) known to sender
Message \(m\) is costless and non-binding
Receiver chooses action \(a\)
Preferences are biased

title: Cheap talk
text:
Core math (quadratic loss, bias)
Let \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \(a\in[0,1]\).
Receiver: \[
u_R=-(a-\theta)^2
\]
Sender (bias \(b>0\)): \[
u_S=-(a-(\theta+b))^2
\]

title: Cheap talk
text:
Equilibrium (what to expect)

There is always a babbling equilibrium: messages convey no information and the receiver chooses a constant action (based on the prior).
When bias is not too large, there are partition equilibria: the sender truthfully reveals which interval \(\theta\) lies in; the receiver responds with the conditional mean of that interval.

title: Cheap talk
text:
Later-on analysis

More alignment → more information: smaller bias typically supports finer partitions.
Credibility via commitment: if the sender could commit to a rule (information design), outcomes change drastically.
Costly messages → signaling: adding costs turns cheap talk into signaling.

title: Signaling games
text: A signaling game is a dynamic game with private information: a sender knows their type, chooses a signal (often costly), then a receiver responds.

title: Signaling games
text: A signaling game is a dynamic game with private information: a sender knows their type, chooses a signal (often costly), then a receiver responds.

title: Signaling games
text:
What’s special

Signals can be credible when different types face different costs/benefits (incentive compatibility).
Typical outcomes: separating (types choose different signals), pooling (same signal), or semi-separating.
Beliefs and off-path beliefs matter (PBE / sequential equilibrium ideas).

title: Signaling games
text:
One example (education as a signal)
Types: high ability \(H\) and low ability \(L\).
Sender chooses education level \(e\ge 0\); receiver (employer) offers wage \(w(e)\).

Education is more costly for \(L\) than \(H\) (single-crossing idea): \[
c_L(e) > c_H(e)\ \text{for } e>0.
\]
Employer wants to pay higher wages if they believe the worker is \(H\).

A separating equilibrium can exist where \(H\) chooses a higher \(e\) and \(L\) chooses a lower \(e\), because mimicking is too costly for \(L\). The signal works because it changes beliefs and is differentially costly.

title: Signaling games
text:
Story
A scholarship committee can’t observe applicant ability directly. Applicants can choose to take a difficult certification exam. High-ability students find it less costly; low-ability students find it very costly. The committee conditions its funding decision on the signal.

title: Signaling games
text:
Model

Types: \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\), prior \(p\)
Signal: \(e\in\{0,1\}\) with costs \(c_H(1)<c_L(1)\) and \(c_H(0)=c_L(0)=0\)
Receiver chooses reward based on beliefs after observing \(e\)

title: Signaling games
text:
Equilibrium (separating vs pooling)
Let the reward be \(w_H\) if perceived high type and \(w_L\) otherwise.
A separating equilibrium with \(H\) choosing \(e=1\) and \(L\) choosing \(e=0\) requires: \[
w_H-c_H(1)\ge w_L
\quad\text{and}\quad
w_H-c_L(1)\le w_L.
\]

title: Signaling games
text:
Later-on analysis

Pooling: if costs aren’t different enough, both types choose the same signal (signal loses meaning).
Off-path beliefs: dynamic equilibrium concepts differ in how they restrict beliefs after unexpected signals.
Continuous effort: allowing \(e\) continuous yields richer separating thresholds and comparative statics.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
What’s special

Focus shifts from equilibrium as a static concept to stability under dynamics.
Key objects: ESS (evolutionarily stable strategy), replicator dynamics, learning rules.
Useful when players are boundedly rational or populations adapt.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
One example (replicator dynamics, 2 strategies)
Let the population share using strategy 1 be \(x\in[0,1]\). If payoffs are \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\), replicator dynamics are:
\[
\dot{x} = x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]
Intuition: the share of a strategy grows when it performs better than the alternative. Fixed points correspond to states where neither strategy has a payoff advantage.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Story
In a large community, newcomers copy behaviors that seem to “work.” Strategies that perform better spread. Nobody solves the game explicitly, yet population patterns evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Model

Strategies are held by a population
Relative payoff determines growth
Dynamics describe how shares change

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Dynamics (replicator)
Let \(x\) be the share playing strategy 1, payoffs \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\): \[
\dot{x}=x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Equilibrium / stability (what to look for)

Rest points satisfy \(\dot{x}=0\) (often \(x=0\), \(x=1\), or where \(\pi_1(x)=\pi_2(x)\)).
Stability depends on whether nearby deviations push \(x\) back or away.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Later-on analysis

ESS: a refinement capturing robustness to mutant invasions.
Learning rules: fictitious play, reinforcement learning, best-response dynamics.
Link to Nash: some dynamics converge to Nash in certain classes of games, but not always.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
What’s special

Many coordination games have multiple equilibria (good/bad outcomes).
Tiny informational frictions can select a unique equilibrium.
Provides a disciplined way to talk about “which equilibrium happens” without arbitrary refinements.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
One example (currency-attack intuition)
A government defends a peg if fundamentals are strong; speculators attack if they expect others to attack.
Each speculator observes a noisy signal of the fundamental. If signals are slightly noisy, an equilibrium often takes a threshold form: attack if your signal is below a cutoff. The cutoff is pinned down endogenously, yielding a unique prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Story
A bank can survive if depositors stay calm, but fails if too many withdraw. Everyone hears rumors, each slightly noisy. If you expect others to run, running is rational; if you expect calm, staying is rational. Multiple equilibria appear.
Global games add tiny private noise and often recover a single “threshold” prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Model

Fundamental \(\theta\) (bank strength)
Private signal: \(x_i=\theta+\varepsilon_i\)
Action: withdraw or stay
Payoffs depend on the fraction withdrawing

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Equilibrium (threshold form, idea)
A typical global-games prediction is: - withdraw iff \(x_i \le x^*\)
The cutoff \(x^*\) solves an indifference condition at which a depositor is just willing to withdraw.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Later-on analysis

Selection: small noise breaks multiplicity and selects one equilibrium.
Policy: transparency and information disclosure can move the cutoff.
Related models: currency attacks, coordination failures, debt rollovers.

title: Extensive-form games
text: An extensive-form game represents timing (who moves when) and information (what players observe) using a game tree.

title: Extensive-form games
text: An extensive-form game represents timing (who moves when) and information (what players observe) using a game tree.

title: Extensive-form games
text:
What’s special

Sequential rationality matters: players optimize at every decision node.
The standard solution is subgame perfect equilibrium via backward induction (perfect information case).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
One example (backward induction)





flowchart TD
  S((Start)) -->|P1: A| A(( ))
  S -->|P1: B| B(( ))
  A -->|P2: L| AL["(2,1)"]
  A -->|P2: R| AR["(0,0)"]
  B -->|P2: L| BL["(1,2)"]
  B -->|P2: R| BR["(3,0)"]






Player 2 chooses L after \(A\) (since \(1>0\)) and L after \(B\) (since \(2>0\)).
Anticipating this, player 1 prefers \(A\) (since \(2>1\)). Outcome: \((A,L)\).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Story
A landlord, Ms. K, is renewing a lease with Rin. The neighborhood has improved, and Ms. K considers raising rent. Ms. K chooses first: a moderate raise or an aggressive one. Rin then decides: accept or move out.
The key is timing: Rin observes the offer before acting, and Ms. K anticipates Rin’s response.

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Model

Player 1 (landlord): \(L\) (low increase) or \(H\) (high increase)
Player 2 (tenant): after observing, \(A\) (accept) or \(M\) (move)
Information: perfect (tenant observes the offer)
Solution concept: backward induction / SPE

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Game tree (toy)





flowchart TD
  S((Start)) -->|P1: L| L(( ))
  S -->|P1: H| H(( ))
  L -->|P2: A| LA["(2,2)"]
  L -->|P2: M| LM["(0,1)"]
  H -->|P2: A| HA["(3,0)"]
  H -->|P2: M| HM["(0,1)"]

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Equilibrium (backward induction → SPE)
Step 1 (tenant’s optimal actions at the second stage): - After \(L\): compare tenant payoff \(2\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → choose \(A\) - After \(H\): compare tenant payoff \(0\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → choose \(M\)
Step 2 (landlord anticipates this): - If choose \(L\) → outcome \((2,2)\) - If choose \(H\) → tenant moves → outcome \((0,1)\)
So landlord chooses \(L\).
SPE outcome: \((L,A)\).

title: Extensive-form games
text:
Later-on analysis

Outside option changes: if moving becomes less costly, the landlord’s ability to raise rent shrinks.
Incomplete information: if Ms. K doesn’t know Rin’s moving cost, the game becomes Bayesian and can generate screening/signaling behavior.
Commitment: if Rin could commit to “move if any increase,” outcomes shift again (commitment changes the tree).

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
What’s special

Timing and outside options shape outcomes.
With discounting, delay is costly → early agreement is attractive.
Incomplete information introduces screening and strategic delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
One example (alternating-offers, intuition)
Two players bargain over splitting 1. In each round, one proposes a split; the other accepts or rejects. If rejected, bargaining continues next round with discount factor \(\delta\).
Backward induction in the infinite-horizon model yields immediate agreement: the proposer offers the responder just enough to make them indifferent between accepting now vs rejecting and waiting. More patient players (higher \(\delta\)) obtain better terms.

title: Bargaining
text:
Story
Two coauthors must decide authorship order before tomorrow’s submission deadline. Delay is costly: missing the deadline reduces the paper’s impact. One proposes a split; the other can accept or reject. If rejected, the other proposes next round.

title: Bargaining
text:
Model

Pie size: 1
Alternating offers
Common discount factor: \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Solution concept: subgame perfect equilibrium

title: Bargaining
text:
Equilibrium (Rubinstein alternating offers, symmetric discounting)
In the infinite-horizon alternating-offers model with the same discount factor \(\delta\) for both players, the unique SPE split is:

First proposer receives: \[
\frac{1}{1+\delta}
\]
Responder receives: \[
\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}.
\]

Intuition: rejecting means you become proposer next round, but you discount the future by \(\delta\).

title: Bargaining
text:
Later-on analysis

Asymmetric patience: if one player has higher \(\delta\), they get a larger share.
Outside options: disagreement payoffs shift the split.
Incomplete information: can generate delay, signaling, and “toughness” reputations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games
Information and mediation (recommendation systems)
Mechanism design / persuasion / traffic routing interpretations
Computational game theory (CE is often easier to compute than NE)

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Choose a distribution over action profiles (a “correlation device”).
For each player and each recommended action, write the no-deviation (obedience) constraints:

expected payoff from following ≥ expected payoff from deviating.

If all obedience constraints hold, the distribution is a correlated equilibrium.

title: Correlated equilibrium
section: Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)
text:
Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)

Problem (context + question)
Two drivers choose routes: \(A\) or \(B\). If both choose the same route, there is congestion and each gets 0. If they choose different routes, each gets 1.
Payoffs: - If actions differ: payoff 1 each - If same: payoff 0 each
Question: Construct a correlated equilibrium that achieves expected payoff 1 for each driver.


Solution
Consider a mediator who flips a fair coin and privately recommends: - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: A, Driver 2: B) - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: B, Driver 2: A)
So the induced distribution puts probability 1/2 on (A,B) and 1/2 on (B,A).
Step 1: Check obedience for Driver 1 - If Driver 1 is told “A”, they infer Driver 2 was told “B”, so following yields payoff 1. Deviating to “B” would match Driver 2 and yield 0. - If Driver 1 is told “B”, symmetric: follow yields 1; deviating yields 0.
So Driver 1 never wants to deviate. Same for Driver 2.
Result: This recommendation device is a correlated equilibrium with payoff 1 for each.


Takeaway
CE allows coordination using signals, often improving welfare relative to uncoordinated play.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Every Nash equilibrium induces a correlated equilibrium (as a special case), but CE can be larger.
CE is closely related to “obedience constraints” in mechanism design.
If you ever do computation: CE can be found via linear programming in finite games.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games when you want predictions weaker than Nash
Settings with equilibrium multiplicity (rationalizability gives a set of plausible actions)
As a foundation for epistemic game theory

title: Rationalizability
section: How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)
text:
How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)

Identify strictly dominated actions for any player and remove them.
Recompute dominance in the reduced game.
Repeat until no more strictly dominated actions remain.
The remaining actions are rationalizable.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Solved example (iterated deletion)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 actions: \(U, M, D\). Player 2 actions: \(L, R\). Payoffs to player 1 are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & 3 & 0\\
M & 2 & 1\\
D & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\]
Assume player 2’s payoffs are irrelevant for this exercise.
Question: Which actions of player 1 are rationalizable by iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies?


Solution
Compare player 1 actions:

Does \(D\) get strictly dominated by \(M\)?

Against \(L\): \(u_1(M)=2 > u_1(D)=1\)
Against \(R\): \(u_1(M)=1 > u_1(D)=0\) Yes: \(M\) strictly dominates \(D\).


So eliminate \(D\).
Now remaining actions for player 1: \(U\) and \(M\). - Does \(U\) strictly dominate \(M\)? No: - Against \(L\): \(U=3 > M=2\) - Against \(R\): \(U=0 < M=1\) - Does \(M\) strictly dominate \(U\)? No, same reason.
Result: The rationalizable actions for player 1 are \(\{U, M\}\).


Takeaway
Rationalizability removes clearly irrational actions but may still leave multiple plausible choices.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Later-on analysis

Nash equilibrium is a stronger prediction than rationalizability.
In some games, iterated strict dominance leads to a unique outcome (then it’s very powerful).
With weak dominance, elimination can depend on order; if you include it, add a warning section.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games with multiple perfect equilibria
Equilibrium selection arguments based on “plausible mistakes”
Advanced micro/game theory refinements

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Start from candidate equilibria (usually Nash / perfect).
Compare payoffs of different deviations.
Impose the idea: probability of a worse deviation is tiny relative to a better deviation.
Check whether the equilibrium can be supported as the limit of such “proper” trembles.

(For most newcomer notes, the key is the intuition, not the full formal definition.)

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Solved example (intuition with unequal mistakes)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 is choosing between three actions \(A,B,C\) against a fixed opponent strategy. Payoffs to player 1 are:

\(u_1(A)=10\) (best)
\(u_1(B)=9\) (slightly worse)
\(u_1(C)=0\) (much worse)

Question: Under the “proper” idea of trembles, which mistake is more plausible: choosing \(B\) or choosing \(C\)?


Solution
Proper equilibrium assumes that when players tremble: - they might mistakenly choose \(B\) instead of \(A\) with small probability, - but choosing \(C\) (which is drastically worse) should be far less likely than choosing \(B\).
So “proper trembles” treat worse errors as exponentially rarer than mild errors.
Result: A proper refinement would allow small probability on \(B\) but push the probability on \(C\) to be negligible relative to \(B\) as trembles vanish.


Check
This matches the guiding principle: the likelihood of mistakes respects payoff ranking and payoff gaps.


Takeaway
Proper equilibrium captures “bounded rationality with common sense”: huge blunders are rarer than small slips.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium ⟹ trembling-hand perfect ⟹ Nash (in finite games).
In practice, proper equilibrium is used when you want a sharper selection than perfection provides.
If you later want a fully formal statement, we can add it as an appendix section.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
A sequential equilibrium is a refinement of PBE. It is a pair (strategies, beliefs) such that:

Sequential rationality: strategies are optimal at every information set given beliefs.
Consistency: beliefs come from strategies via Bayes’ rule as limits of fully mixed (“trembling”) strategies.

This “tremble” requirement disciplines off-path beliefs: beliefs must be justifiable by small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
A sequential equilibrium is a refinement of PBE. It is a pair (strategies, beliefs) such that:

Sequential rationality: strategies are optimal at every information set given beliefs.
Consistency: beliefs come from strategies via Bayes’ rule as limits of fully mixed (“trembling”) strategies.

This “tremble” requirement disciplines off-path beliefs: beliefs must be justifiable by small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Signaling games and dynamic games with imperfect information
Any setting where PBE has many equilibria due to arbitrary off-path beliefs
Refinement discussions in micro theory / game theory texts

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Start from a candidate PBE.
Add small probabilities (trembles) so every action is played with positive probability.
Compute beliefs via Bayes’ rule under the perturbed strategy.
Take limits as trembles go to zero:

if beliefs converge, they are consistent.

Check sequential rationality with those beliefs.

title: Sequential equilibrium
section: Solved example (why some off-path beliefs are not credible)
text:
Solved example (why some off-path beliefs are not credible)

Problem (context + question)
Consider the pooling PBE from the PBE page: - Both types choose \(e=0\). - Off-path belief after \(e=1\) is \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\).
Question: Explain the consistency idea: what must be true for such an off-path belief to be allowed under sequential equilibrium?


Solution
Sequential equilibrium requires off-path beliefs to be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed strategies.
So imagine a perturbed (trembling) strategy where: - Type \(H\) plays \(e=1\) with small probability \(\varepsilon_H>0\), - Type \(L\) plays \(e=1\) with small probability \(\varepsilon_L>0\).
Then, upon observing \(e=1\), Bayes’ rule gives: \[
\Pr(H\mid e=1)=\frac{p\,\varepsilon_H}{p\,\varepsilon_H+(1-p)\,\varepsilon_L}.
\]
Now consider the limit as trembles vanish. The limiting belief depends on the relative rate at which \(\varepsilon_H\) and \(\varepsilon_L\) go to zero.

If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to 0\), then \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)\to 0\).
If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to \infty\), then \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)\to 1\).
If \(\varepsilon_H/\varepsilon_L \to k\in(0,\infty)\), then the limit is an interior number in \((0,1)\).

Result: The off-path belief \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\) is consistent only if the perturbations imply that, in the limit, type \(H\) is vanishingly less likely than type \(L\) to make that mistake.


Check
This belief is not “free”: it must be explainable by a sequence of fully mixed strategies.


Takeaway
Sequential equilibrium restricts off-path beliefs by requiring them to arise from plausible small mistakes.

title: Sequential equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Sequential equilibrium is often closer to how theorists think about “reasonable beliefs” off-path.
Stronger refinements (e.g., intuitive criterion) impose additional structure.
For applied work, PBE is common; for selection arguments, sequential equilibrium is a useful upgrade.

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player can gain by deviating unilaterally.

How to solve (recipe)

Pure strategies

(Optional) Check for strict dominance and eliminate dominated actions.
Compute each player’s best response to every opponent action.
Nash equilibria are intersections of best responses.



Mixed strategies (2×2 or small games)

Guess supports (which actions get positive probability).

title: Nash equilibrium (NE)
text:
Solved example (pure NE)

Problem (context + question)
Two cafés simultaneously choose discount \(D\) or normal pricing \(N\). Payoffs are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& D & N\\ \hline
D & (1,1) & (3,0)\\
N & (0,3) & (2,2)
\end{array}
\]
Question: Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria.


Solution
Step 1 (player 1 best responses): - If player 2 plays \(D\), player 1 compares \(1\) (play \(D\)) vs \(0\) (play \(N\)) → best response is \(D\). - If player 2 plays \(N\), player 1 compares \(3\) (play \(D\)) vs \(2\) (play \(N\)) → best response is \(D\).
So player 1’s best response is always \(D\).
Step 2 (player 2 best responses): By symmetry, player 2’s best response is always \(D\).
Result: The unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\).


Check
At \((D,D)\), deviating to \(N\) reduces each café’s payoff from \(1\) to \(0\).


Takeaway
NE can be inefficient: both cafés would prefer \((N,N)\), but strategic incentives push them to discount.

Refinements: in dynamic games, Nash can allow non-credible threats → motivates SPE.
Correlated equilibrium: enlarges the solution concept by allowing correlation devices.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
A set \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is convex if for any \(x,y\in C\) and any \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y \in C.
\]
Intuition. If you can take “mixtures” of two feasible points and stay feasible, the set is convex. This is exactly why mixed strategies live in a simplex.

title: Convexity & concavity
text:
Concave functions
A function \(f\) is concave on a convex set if for any \(x,y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y)\ge \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda)f(y).
\]
Intuition. Concavity means “diminishing returns” and makes optimization well-behaved: local maxima are global.

title: Convexity & concavity
section: Example: why concavity helps best responses
text:
Example: why concavity helps best responses
Let \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) on \([0,2]\). Then \(f''(x)=-2<0\), so \(f\) is concave and the maximizer is unique.
FOC: \(f'(x)=2-2x=0 \Rightarrow x^*=1\).
In games, concavity in your own action often implies a unique best response.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
\(\sigma\)-algebra (concept only)
Let \(\Omega\) be the set of possible states of the world.
A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) is a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events) such that:

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(A^c \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_k \in \mathcal{F}\)

Intuition. \(\mathcal{F}\) lists the events you are able to talk about (and condition on).
Coarser \(\mathcal{F}\) = less information.

Finite shortcut (partition view)
If \(\Omega\) is finite and a player’s information is a partition \[
\Pi = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\},
\] then the player can distinguish only which cell \(C_j\) contains the true state.
The corresponding \(\sigma\)-algebra is “all unions of cells of \(\Pi\)”.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
text:
Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
Given an integrable random variable \(X\) (e.g., payoff-relevant quantity) and an information set \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) is the random variable that represents the best mean-squared prediction of \(X\) using only information in \(\mathcal{G}\).
Projection idea (intuition). Think of \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) as projecting \(X\) onto the space of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable variables (things you can compute using the information you have).

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Example: conditional expectation with a partition
text:
Example: conditional expectation with a partition
Let the state space be \[
\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\omega_k)=\tfrac14 \text{ for each }k.
\]
Let \[
X(\omega_1)=0,\;X(\omega_2)=2,\;X(\omega_3)=4,\;X(\omega_4)=6.
\]
Suppose the player only observes whether the state is in \[
C_1=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\quad\text{or}\quad C_2=\{\omega_3,\omega_4\}.
\]
That information corresponds to a partition \(\Pi=\{C_1,C_2\}\) (and a \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by it).
Then the conditional expectation is constant on each cell:

On \(C_1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_1]
=\frac{X(\omega_1)+X(\omega_2)}{2}
=\frac{0+2}{2}=1.
\]
On \(C_2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_2]
=\frac{X(\omega_3)+X(\omega_4)}{2}
=\frac{4+6}{2}=5.
\]

So \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) takes value \(1\) if you learn “cell \(C_1\)”, and value \(5\) if you learn “cell \(C_2\)”.
Game theory interpretation. This is exactly what beliefs do: you map what you observed to an updated expectation of payoff-relevant quantities.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Common knowledge (concept)
An event \(E\) is common knowledge if: - everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - and so on indefinitely.
Intuition. Common knowledge is what makes coordination possible (or impossible). It is stronger than “everyone knows”.

Iterated beliefs (one-line idea)
In Bayesian games, strategies can depend on: - beliefs about types, - beliefs about others’ beliefs, - higher-order beliefs.
Often you don’t compute these explicitly; you just need to know they exist and that equilibrium concepts impose consistency.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Practical takeaway
For most game theory work: - partitions are enough to model information, - conditional expectation captures “best prediction given what you know”, - common knowledge / higher-order beliefs matter conceptually for coordination and equilibrium.

title: Linear algebra
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure actions. If player \(i\) has \(m\) pure actions, a mixed strategy is
\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]
the \((m-1)\)-simplex.
Intuition. You can think of \(x\) as a “weighting” of actions. The simplex condition just says: nonnegative weights that sum to 1.

title: Linear algebra
text:

\[
\Delta^{m-1}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:\; x_k\ge 0\;\forall k,\;\sum_{k=1}^m x_k = 1\right\},
\]

title: Linear algebra
text:
Payoff matrices and expected payoff
In a two-player normal-form game, let player 1 have \(m\) actions and player 2 have \(n\) actions. Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be player 1’s payoff matrix (and \(B\) for player 2). If player 1 plays \(x\in\Delta^{m-1}\) and player 2 plays \(y\in\Delta^{n-1}\), then player 1’s expected payoff is
\[
u_1(x,y)=x^\top A y.
\]
Intuition. First compute expected payoffs against each of player 2’s pure actions (\(Ay\)). Then average those numbers using player 1’s mixing weights (\(x^\top\)).

title: Linear algebra
text:
Example: 2×2 game
Suppose
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{pmatrix}0.4\\0.6\end{pmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{pmatrix}0.25\\0.75\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
Ay=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 0\\
1 & 3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
0.25\\0.75
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5\\
2.5
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_1(x,y)=x^\top(Ay)=0.4\cdot 0.5+0.6\cdot 2.5=1.7.
\]
So the mixed-vs-mixed expected payoff is \(1.7\) for player 1.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
A fixed point of a function \(f:X\to X\) is a point \(x^*\) such that \[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:

\]
Intuition. An equilibrium is often a fixed point: if “best response” maps strategies into strategies, equilibrium is where nothing changes.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Brouwer (idea)
Brouwer’s fixed point theorem (informal): a continuous function from a compact convex set to itself has a fixed point.
This supports existence of equilibrium in many continuous games.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Correspondences (set-valued maps)
A correspondence \(F:X \rightrightarrows X\) assigns a set \(F(x)\) to each \(x\). Best responses are usually correspondences: \[
BR_i(s_{-i}) = \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}),
\] which may contain multiple maximizers.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Kakutani (idea)
Kakutani’s theorem (informal): under continuity-like conditions and nonempty convex values, a correspondence has a fixed point: \[
x^* \in F(x^*).
\]
This is the classic route to Nash existence with mixed strategies: the product of best-response correspondences has a fixed point.

title: Fixed points & correspondences
text:
Example: fixed point intuition in 1D
Let \(f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\) on \([0,1]\). Solve \(x=f(x)\): \[
x=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{4}\Rightarrow x^*=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Equilibrium-as-fixed-point is exactly this: apply the rule, you land back on yourself.

title: Probability
text:
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions. If the action set is finite, this is just a probability vector (see the simplex definition in Linear algebra).
Intuition. “Randomizing” in game theory is not mystical: it’s a distribution that other players can form beliefs about.

title: Probability

title: Probability
text:
Expectation
If a random variable \(X\) takes values \(x_k\) with probabilities \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k x_k p_k.
\]
In games, expected utility under a mixed strategy is exactly this idea: average the payoff over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.

title: Probability
text:
Bayes’ rule
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\,\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
\]
Intuition. Prior belief \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) gets updated by how well \(A\) predicts the evidence \(B\).

title: Probability
text:
Example: updating beliefs about types
A player is either type \(H\) or \(L\). Prior \(\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{P}(L)=0.7\). You observe a signal \(s\). Suppose
\[
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)=0.8,\qquad \mathbb{P}(s\mid L)=0.2.
\]
First compute the overall likelihood of \(s\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)=\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)+\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)\mathbb{P}(L)=0.8\cdot 0.3+0.2\cdot 0.7=0.38.
\]
Then the posterior belief is
\[
\mathbb{P}(H\mid s)=\frac{0.8\cdot 0.3}{0.38}\approx 0.6316.
\]
So after observing \(s\), belief in type \(H\) rises from \(0.3\) to about \(0.63\).

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
A best response is an optimization problem. Given others’ strategies \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})\in \arg\max_{s_i\in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
Intuition. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of best responses: everyone is already choosing an argmax given others.

title: Optimization
text:
FOC / SOC (unconstrained)
If \(f\) is differentiable and you maximize over an interval, an interior optimum \(x^*\) satisfies the first-order condition (FOC)
\[
f'(x^*)=0.
\]
If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the second-order condition (SOC) for a local maximum is
\[
f''(x^*)<0.
\]
Intuition. FOC finds stationary points; SOC checks that the curve bends downward.

title: Optimization
text:
KKT conditions (constrained)
For maximizing \(f(x)\) subject to inequality constraints \(g_j(x)\le 0\), define the Lagrangian
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\sum_{j}\lambda_j g_j(x),
\qquad \lambda_j\ge 0.
\]
KKT conditions (at an optimum, under standard regularity assumptions) include: - Stationarity: \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*,\lambda^*)=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(g_j(x^*)\le 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda_j^*\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0\) for all \(j\)
Intuition. Constraints either bind (then they get a positive “shadow price” \(\lambda_j\)) or don’t bind (then \(\lambda_j=0\)).

title: Optimization
section: Example: best response with a constraint
text:
Example: best response with a constraint
Maximize \(f(x)=2x-x^2\) subject to \(x\ge 0\).
Write the constraint as \(g(x)=-x\le 0\). Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)= (2x-x^2)-\lambda(-x)=2x-x^2+\lambda x.
\]
KKT: - Stationarity: \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=2-2x+\lambda=0\) - Primal feasibility: \(x\ge 0\) - Dual feasibility: \(\lambda\ge 0\) - Complementary slackness: \(\lambda x=0\)
From stationarity: \(2-2x+\lambda=0 \Rightarrow x=1+\lambda/2\).
If \(x>0\), then complementary slackness implies \(\lambda=0\), so \(x=1\). Check feasibility: \(1\ge 0\) yes. So the solution is \(x^*=1\).
(If the unconstrained maximizer had been negative, the constraint would bind and you’d get \(x^*=0\) with \(\lambda>0\).)

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
A Bayesian game has private information (types). A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs about others’ types.
Formally, each player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\) and chooses an action via a strategy \(s_i(\theta_i)\). A BNE satisfies, for each type \(\theta_i\): \[
s_i(\theta_i)\in \arg\max_{a_i} \mathbb{E}\left[u_i(a_i, s_{-i}(\theta_{-i}), \theta_i,\theta_{-i})\mid \theta_i\right].
\]

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Where it shows up

Static games of incomplete information (entry games, pricing with private costs)
Auctions (many auction models are BNE)
As the static benchmark for dynamic incomplete-information models

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

List types and prior beliefs.
Write strategies as functions of types: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
Compute each type’s expected payoff from each action.
Choose best responses by type.
Verify mutual best responses given beliefs.

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Solved example (type-dependent best response)

Problem (context + question)
An investor chooses whether to fund a startup: \(F\) (fund) or \(R\) (reject).
The startup’s type is \(\theta\in\{S,W\}\) (strong or weak), with prior \(\Pr(S)=p\). If the investor funds: - payoff is \(+1\) if \(\theta=S\), - payoff is \(-1\) if \(\theta=W\).
If the investor rejects, payoff is \(0\).
Question: Find the investor’s optimal action as a function of \(p\) (a BNE decision rule).


Solution
Compute expected payoff from funding: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi(F)] = p(1) + (1-p)(-1) = 2p-1.
\]
Rejecting yields: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi(R)] = 0.
\]
So the investor funds iff \(2p-1\ge 0\), i.e. \[
p \ge \tfrac12.
\]
Result: Optimal strategy is: - choose \(F\) if \(p\ge 1/2\), - choose \(R\) if \(p<1/2\), - indifferent at \(p=1/2\).


Check
Given beliefs (the prior), the chosen action maximizes expected payoff.


Takeaway
BNE decisions are often threshold rules: act if expected benefit given beliefs is large enough.

title: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)
text:
Later-on analysis

If a signal is observed before acting, beliefs update via Bayes’ rule and the threshold shifts.
If the informed party can strategically choose information, you move toward signaling or cheap talk → PBE.
With many types/actions, equilibrium often has cutoff strategies and monotonicity structure.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
A trembling-hand perfect equilibrium (perfect equilibrium) is a Nash equilibrium that remains optimal when every player might make tiny mistakes (“trembles”).
Formally (intuition-level): a strategy profile is perfect if it is the limit of a sequence of fully mixed strategy profiles (every action played with positive probability) where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others in that sequence.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games where Nash equilibria include weakly dominated or non-robust behavior
Refinement arguments: “Would this equilibrium survive small mistakes?”
Often discussed alongside proper equilibrium and sequential equilibrium

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Why it exists (intuition)
If an equilibrium relies on assigning zero probability to “unlikely” actions, trembles force you to confront those actions. Strategies that are only optimal because some opponent action is assumed impossible may fail perfection.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Find Nash equilibria.
Check whether an equilibrium uses weakly dominated strategies or fragile best responses.
Consider small trembles: assume each player plays every action with tiny probability.
Ask: is the equilibrium strategy still a best response when opponents sometimes tremble?
If yes (as a limit), it’s perfect.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
section: Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)
text:
Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)

Problem (context + question)
Consider this 2×2 game (payoffs shown as (player 1, player 2)):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & (1,1) & (0,1)\\
D & (1,0) & (0,0)
\end{array}
\]
Question: (i) Find all Nash equilibria. (ii) Which are trembling-hand perfect?


Solution
Step 1: Best responses - Player 1: - If player 2 plays \(L\): payoff from \(U\) is 1, from \(D\) is 1 → both \(U\) and \(D\) are best responses. - If player 2 plays \(R\): payoff from \(U\) is 0, from \(D\) is 0 → both are best responses. - Player 2: - If player 1 plays \(U\): payoffs are 1 from \(L\) and 1 from \(R\) → both best responses. - If player 1 plays \(D\): payoffs are 0 from \(L\) and 0 from \(R\) → both best responses.
So every pure profile is a Nash equilibrium (players are indifferent everywhere).
Step 2: Add trembles Suppose player 2 trembles: plays \(L\) with probability \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(R\) with probability \(\varepsilon>0\).
Player 1’s expected payoff from: - \(U\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\) - \(D\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\)
Still indifferent. So trembles do not break player 1’s indifference.
Now suppose player 1 trembles: plays \(U\) with probability \(1-\delta\) and \(D\) with probability \(\delta>0\).
Player 2’s expected payoff from: - \(L\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\) - \(R\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\)
Still indifferent.
Result: In this particular game, trembles do not select: equilibria are robust because payoffs create genuine indifference.


Takeaway
Perfection rules out equilibria that only work by assuming “impossible” actions never happen. But if the game truly makes players indifferent, perfection won’t refine further.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium strengthens perfection by making “worse mistakes” exponentially less likely.
In extensive-form games, sequential equilibrium is the tremble-based refinement with beliefs.
In many applied models, perfection is used to exclude equilibria involving weakly dominated actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Nash equilibrium (NE)

Pure NE

(Optional) Remove strictly dominated actions.
Compute best responses.
Intersections of best responses = pure NE.



Mixed NE (quick 2×2 method)
Let player 1 mix \(p\) on \(U\) (and \(1-p\) on \(D\)). Let player 2 mix \(q\) on \(L\) (and \(1-q\) on \(R\)). 1) Make player 1 indifferent between \(U\) and \(D\) → solve for \(q\). 2) Make player 2 indifferent between \(L\) and \(R\) → solve for \(p\). 3) Check \(p,q\in[0,1]\) and supports are consistent.
Common pitfall: mixing is only required when the opponent is indifferent among the actions in their support.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)

Backward induction (finite perfect-information trees)

Start at the last decision nodes.
Choose optimal action there.
Replace that subgame with its continuation payoff.
Move backward until the root.

Common pitfall: using non-credible threats (actions that wouldn’t be optimal if reached).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)

Write types and prior \(\Pr(\theta)\).
Strategy is type-contingent: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
For each type, compute expected payoff for each action.
Choose best responses for each type; verify consistency across players.

Common pitfall: forgetting strategies are functions of type, not single actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
A PBE is (strategies, beliefs) satisfying: - Sequential rationality: actions optimal at every information set. - Bayes consistency on-path: update beliefs using Bayes’ rule where possible.

Standard workflow (signaling/screening)

Guess form: separating / pooling / semi-separating.
Propose strategies for sender types + receiver actions.
Compute on-path posteriors via Bayes.
Check receiver best responses given beliefs.
Check each sender type’s incentive constraints (no profitable deviations).
Specify off-path beliefs (carefully) and re-check deviations.

Common pitfall: not stating off-path beliefs, or using off-path beliefs that “magically” punish deviations without justification (sequential equilibrium addresses this).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Sequential equilibrium (SE)
Sequential equilibrium is PBE + a discipline on beliefs: - Beliefs must be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed trembles.

Practical use
If your PBE relies heavily on off-path beliefs: 1) Add tiny tremble probabilities to every action. 2) Compute implied posteriors. 3) Take limits → see which beliefs are justifiable. 4) Re-check optimality.
Common pitfall: treating off-path beliefs as completely free.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)

Receiver ignores message: same action after every message.
Beliefs stay at the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring).
Sender is indifferent over messages because messages don’t affect actions.

Use: baseline; compare informative equilibria against it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium

Start from a Nash equilibrium.
Ask whether it survives when opponents sometimes make small mistakes.
Equilibria relying on “impossible” actions not happening can fail.

Heuristic: if an equilibrium uses weakly dominated actions or fragile indifference, perfection may eliminate it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Proper equilibrium
Like perfect equilibrium, but: - very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad mistakes.
Use: sharper selection when perfection is not selective enough.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Correlated equilibrium (CE)

Specify a distribution over action profiles (recommendations).
For each player and each recommendation, write obedience constraints: following ≥ deviating.
If all constraints hold, it’s a CE.

Memory aid: “Follow the recommendation because conditional on it, deviating doesn’t help.”

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Rationalizability

Iteratively delete strictly dominated actions.
Repeat in the reduced game until no more deletions.
Remaining actions are rationalizable.

Common pitfall: weak dominance deletion can be order-dependent (start with strict).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Mini glossary (quick)

NE: best response to best response.
SPE: NE in every subgame (credible).
BNE: NE with types; best response in expectation.
PBE: strategies + beliefs; Bayes on-path; sequentially rational.
SE: PBE + tremble-consistent beliefs.
CE: equilibrium over distributions; “obey the signal.”
Rationalizability: what survives iterated strict dominance.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Where it shows up

Cheap talk models (sender–receiver)
Communication settings with strong preference misalignment
As the “uninformative” benchmark when discussing informative equilibria (partition, separating)

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Make the receiver ignore messages: choose the same action after any message.
Set receiver beliefs equal to the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring messages).
Verify receiver optimality under those beliefs.
Verify sender indifference: since messages don’t affect actions, any message is optimal.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Solved example (fully worked)

Problem (context + question)
A sender observes \(\theta\in\{0,1\}\) with prior \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Sender sends costless message \(m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}\). Receiver chooses action \(a\in\{0,1\}\).
Receiver payoff: \[
u_R(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=\theta\}.
\]
Sender payoff (biased toward \(a=1\)): \[
u_S(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=1\}.
\]
Question: Exhibit a babbling equilibrium (strategies + beliefs) and verify it.


Solution
A babbling equilibrium has receiver ignore the message.
Step 1 (receiver best response when ignoring messages): Under the prior, \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Then - payoff from \(a=1\) is \(1/2\), - payoff from \(a=0\) is \(1/2\).
Receiver is indifferent, so a valid best response is: \[
a=0 \quad \text{after both messages}.
\]
Step 2 (sender incentives): If the receiver always plays \(a=0\), sender payoff is always \(0\) regardless of message. So the sender is indifferent and can send any message.
Let sender strategy be: always send “high”.
Step 3 (beliefs): Receiver beliefs do not depend on the message (since messages are ignored). Keep the prior: \[
\Pr(\theta=1\mid m)=1/2 \quad \text{for both } m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}.
\]
Result (babbling equilibrium): - Sender: always send “high”. - Receiver: always choose \(a=0\). - Beliefs: posterior equals prior after any message.


Check

Receiver optimality: given prior, \(a=0\) is a best response (ties).
Sender optimality: given receiver ignores messages, any message is optimal.
Beliefs are consistent with the equilibrium (receiver does not condition on \(m\)).



Takeaway
Babbling equilibria always exist because cheap messages can be ignored.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Later-on analysis

Informative equilibria require structure: partial alignment, restrictions on message space, or repeated interaction.
Adding costs converts cheap talk into signaling, where credibility can be restored.
Many refinements aim to rule out “unreasonable” beliefs or equilibria, but babbling is a genuine equilibrium prediction in many environments.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Where it shows up

Signaling games (education, quality signals)
Screening models with dynamic interaction
Any extensive-form game with imperfect information

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Guess an equilibrium form (separating / pooling / semi-separating).
Specify strategies for all players.
Derive beliefs using Bayes’ rule on-path.
Check sequential rationality at every information set:

receiver best-responds given beliefs,
sender type best-responds given receiver strategy.

Specify off-path beliefs and verify no profitable deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
section: Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)
text:
Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)

Problem (context + question)
Types: worker \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) with \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Worker chooses education \(e\in\{0,1\}\). Employer observes \(e\) and offers wage \(w\in\{w_H,w_L\}\).
Productivity: - If type \(H\): output value is \(2\) - If type \(L\): output value is \(1\)
Employer is competitive and pays expected productivity given beliefs: - pay \(w_H=2\) if believes \(H\) for sure, - pay \(w_L=1\) if believes \(L\) for sure, - pay \(w=p\cdot 2+(1-p)\cdot 1 = 1+p\) if belief is \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Education costs: - \(c_H(1)=0.2\), \(c_L(1)=0.8\), and \(c_H(0)=c_L(0)=0\).
Question: Construct a pooling PBE where both types choose \(e=0\).


Solution
We propose a pooling strategy: - Worker: \(e(\theta)=0\) for both \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\). - Employer: after observing \(e=0\), pay \(w(0)=1+p\) (belief equals prior); after \(e=1\), specify an off-path belief.
Step 1 (beliefs on-path): Since both types choose \(e=0\), observing \(e=0\) yields posterior \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\). So paying \(w(0)=1+p\) is consistent.
Step 2 (employer sequential rationality): Given belief \(p\) after \(e=0\), competitive wage is \(1+p\). Good.
Now choose an off-path belief after \(e=1\). Let employer believe \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\) (i.e., “only low types deviate”), so employer pays \(w(1)=1\).
Step 3 (worker incentive constraints): - Type \(H\) payoff if follow pooling (\(e=0\)): \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.2\) → \(1-0.2=0.8\). So \(H\) does not deviate if \(1+p \ge 0.8\), which holds for all \(p\in[0,1]\).

Type \(L\) payoff if follow pooling: \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.8\) → \(0.2\). So \(L\) never deviates.

Result (pooling PBE): - Worker: both types choose \(e=0\). - Employer beliefs: \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\); off-path set \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\). - Employer wages: \(w(0)=1+p\), \(w(1)=1\).


Check

Beliefs on-path follow Bayes’ rule.
Actions are optimal at each information set given beliefs. So it is a PBE.



Takeaway
PBE requires beliefs; off-path beliefs can support pooling by punishing deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Later-on analysis

Pooling PBEs can be fragile: refinements (sequential equilibrium, intuitive criterion) restrict off-path beliefs.
Separating PBEs require incentive compatibility inequalities (high type willing to signal; low type not).
PBE is a practical workhorse; just be explicit about beliefs and on/off-path behavior.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Where it shows up

Extensive-form games with perfect information (classic backward induction)
Dynamic games where credibility of threats/promises matters
Bargaining models (alternating offers) are solved using SPE

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Identify subgames (in perfect-information games, every decision node typically starts a subgame).
Solve the last subgames first (optimize at terminal decision nodes).
Replace each solved subgame by its continuation payoff.
Continue backward until the start: this is backward induction.
The resulting strategy profile is an SPE (in finite perfect-information games).

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Solved example (backward induction)

Problem (context + question)
A landlord (player 1) offers a rent increase: \(L\) (low) or \(H\) (high). The tenant (player 2) observes and chooses accept \(A\) or move \(M\).
Payoffs: - \((L,A)=(2,2)\), \((L,M)=(0,1)\) - \((H,A)=(3,0)\), \((H,M)=(0,1)\)
Question: Find the SPE.


Solution
Step 1 (solve tenant’s decision in each subgame): - After \(L\): tenant compares payoff \(2\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(A\). - After \(H\): tenant compares payoff \(0\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(M\).
So tenant strategy is: after \(L\) play \(A\), after \(H\) play \(M\).
Step 2 (landlord anticipates tenant’s response): - If landlord chooses \(L\), outcome is \((2,2)\). - If landlord chooses \(H\), tenant moves, outcome is \((0,1)\).
Landlord prefers \(L\) because \(2>0\).
Result (SPE): - Landlord plays \(L\). - Tenant plays \(A\) after \(L\) and \(M\) after \(H\). - Outcome: \((L,A)\).


Check

Tenant’s actions are optimal in each subgame.
Given tenant’s strategy, landlord’s choice is optimal at the start. So the strategy profile is Nash in every subgame.



Takeaway
SPE rules out non-credible threats by requiring optimal behavior after every history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Later-on analysis

With imperfect information, “subgame” may not be well-defined → PBE / sequential equilibrium.
With multiple SPE, equilibrium selection becomes a separate question.
In repeated games, SPE sets are large; punishments must still be credible.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text:
What’s special

Past behavior can be rewarded/punished → enables cooperation even when the one-shot game would not.
Central ideas: incentives over time, credibility, and equilibrium path vs off-path threats.
Infinite-horizon models often use a discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\).

title: Repeated games
section: One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
text:
One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Stage game: cooperate \(C\) or defect \(D\). Typical payoffs: - \((C,C)\) gives \((R,R)\), - \((D,C)\) gives \((T,S)\), - \((C,D)\) gives \((S,T)\), - \((D,D)\) gives \((P,P)\), with \(T>R>P>S\).
Grim trigger strategy: start with \(C\), continue \(C\) unless someone defects; after any defection, play \(D\) forever.
Incentive condition (intuition): cooperate today if the present temptation \(T-R\) is outweighed by the discounted future loss from punishment. Cooperation can be sustained if \(\delta\) is sufficiently high.

title: Repeated games
text:
Story
Two graduate students, Kai and Mira, share an office. Each week they decide whether to clean the shared space. Cleaning is effortful; skipping is tempting. If one keeps cleaning while the other skips, resentment builds. If both skip, the office becomes miserable.
Because the choice repeats, today’s action can trigger tomorrow’s response.

title: Repeated games
text:
Model

Stage actions: \(C\) (clean), \(S\) (shirk)
Stage payoffs (toy): PD-like
Infinite horizon with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Strategies can condition on history

title: Repeated games
text:
Equilibrium (cooperation via grim trigger)
Grim trigger: play \(C\) unless someone shirks; after any shirking, play \(S\) forever.
Compare deviating once vs cooperating on-path (player 1, symmetric): - Cooperate forever payoff: \(\frac{2}{1-\delta}\) - Deviate once (get 3 now, then punished with 1 forever): \(3 + \frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\)
Cooperation is sustainable if: \[
\frac{2}{1-\delta} \ge 3+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta \ge \frac12.
\]

title: Repeated games
text:
Later-on analysis

Finite horizon: backward induction kills cooperation near the end (unless there are other frictions).
Noisy actions: if mistakes happen, harsh punishments can be inefficient; “forgiving” strategies (tit-for-tat variants) become relevant.
Multiple equilibria: repeated games often admit many equilibrium paths; selection becomes a real question.

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text:
What’s special

Bidding strategies trade off winning probability vs payment.
In private values with risk-neutral bidders, many formats have linked outcomes (revenue equivalence under conditions).
In common-value settings, bidders fear the winner’s curse.

title: Auctions
text:
One example (second-price auction, private values)
Each bidder has value \(v_i\) for the item. In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i = v_i.
\]
Intuition: your bid only affects whether you win, not what you pay conditional on winning. Overbidding risks winning at a price above your value; underbidding risks losing when you would have profited.

title: Auctions
text:
Story
A tutor releases one Saturday slot. Many students bid; each has private urgency. The rule for who pays what shapes bidding incentives.

title: Auctions
text:
Model

Bidders \(i=1,\dots,n\)
Private values \(v_i\)
Bids \(b_i\)
Auction format determines allocation and payment

title: Auctions
text:
Equilibrium (second-price auction)
In a second-price auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i=v_i.
\]
Reason (one-line): your bid affects winning, but the price conditional on winning is the opponent’s bid, not yours.

title: Auctions
text:
Later-on analysis

First-price auctions: equilibrium involves bid shading; risk aversion matters.
Common values: winner’s curse and information aggregation dominate.
Reserve prices and optimal design: mechanism design connects auctions to revenue maximization.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
What’s special

Strategies are complete plans chosen at once (pure or mixed).
Main solution concept: Nash equilibrium (possibly mixed).
Workhorse tools: best responses, dominance, indifference.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
One example (Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Actions: \(C\) (cooperate) or \(D\) (defect).
Payoffs: - \((C,C)=(2,2)\) - \((D,C)=(3,0)\) - \((C,D)=(0,3)\) - \((D,D)=(1,1)\)
Solution sketch. \(D\) strictly dominates \(C\) for each player, so the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\), even though \((C,C)\) is Pareto-better.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Story
Two independent cafés, North Bean and South Bean, sit across the same narrow street by a commuter station. Tomorrow morning there will be a marathon: heavy demand, impatient customers, and intense competition for foot traffic. Tonight, each café must decide whether to run a deep discount.
If only one café discounts, it steals attention and most walk-ins. If both discount, they split the crowd but both suffer thin margins. If neither discounts, both do fine—yet each fears being the only one who doesn’t discount.
They decide simultaneously: no café observes the other’s choice before committing.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Model

Players: cafés \(1,2\)
Actions: \(D\) (discount), \(N\) (normal)
Timing: simultaneous
Payoffs: profits

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Payoffs (toy)
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& D & N\\ \hline
D & (1,1) & (3,0)\\
N & (0,3) & (2,2)
\end{array}
\]

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Equilibrium (Nash)
Best responses: - If the other chooses \(N\), your best response is \(D\) (you gain market share). - If the other chooses \(D\), your best response is \(D\) (you avoid being undercut).
So \(D\) is a best response to both opponent actions: the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Later-on analysis

Why it matters: this is the basic logic behind price wars and “race to the bottom” outcomes.
If repeated: repeated interaction can sustain \((N,N)\) via punishments (see Repeated games).
If asymmetric costs: one café might never discount, shifting equilibrium and welfare.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text:
What’s special

Local interactions can produce global patterns (cascades, clusters).
Strategic complements/substitutes on a graph lead to amplification or dampening.
Network position (centrality) can predict influence and equilibrium actions.

title: Network games
text:
One example (linear-quadratic network game)
Let \(G\) be an adjacency matrix and actions \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A common form is:
\[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i - \frac12 a_i^2 + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_i a_j.
\]
FOC for each \(i\) gives: \[
a_i = \alpha + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_j.
\]
In vector form: \[
a = \alpha \mathbf{1} + \beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a = (I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha \mathbf{1},
\] when \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible.
Intuition: your action responds to neighbors; the network structure shapes equilibrium via the matrix inverse.

title: Network games
text:
Story
Study effort spreads through friendships: when your neighbors study more, you feel pressure and motivation. Your best response depends on your local network, and the network structure shapes the overall pattern.

title: Network games
text:
Model

Players are nodes in a graph with adjacency matrix \(G\)
Each chooses action \(a_i\)
Payoff has spillovers with neighbors

title: Network games
text:
Equilibrium (linear-quadratic network game)
Utility: \[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i-\frac12 a_i^2+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_i a_j.
\]
FOC: \[
a_i=\alpha+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_j.
\]
Vector form: \[
a=\alpha\mathbf 1+\beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a=(I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha\mathbf 1,
\] provided \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible (a common sufficient condition is \(|\beta|<1/\rho(G)\) where \(\rho(G)\) is the spectral radius).

title: Network games
text:
Later-on analysis

Complements vs substitutes: sign of \(\beta\) changes amplification vs dampening.
Centrality: equilibrium actions often correlate with network centrality.
Interventions: targeted subsidies/penalties can propagate through the network.

title: Bayesian games
text:
A Bayesian game models incomplete information: players have private types and hold beliefs about others’ types.
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs.

title: Bayesian games
text:
A Bayesian game models incomplete information: players have private types and hold beliefs about others’ types.
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs.

title: Bayesian games
text:
What’s special

Strategies map types to actions.
Beliefs (priors/posteriors) drive behavior.
Same strategic logic as normal-form games, but with expectations over types.

title: Bayesian games
text:
One example (2-type entry game)
Player 1 (incumbent) has type \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(H)=p\). Player 2 (entrant) chooses \(E\) (enter) or \(O\) (out). If entrant stays out: payoffs \((1,0)\).
If entrant enters: - If type is \(H\): fight is profitable for incumbent. - If type is \(L\): accommodate is better.
Toy payoff if entrant enters: - Type \(H\) incumbent prefers Fight, giving entrant payoff \(-1\). - Type \(L\) incumbent prefers Accommodate, giving entrant payoff \(+1\).
Entrant enters if expected payoff is nonnegative: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi_2 \mid E] = p(-1) + (1-p)(+1) = 1-2p \ge 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad p \le \frac12.
\]
Solution sketch. The entrant’s decision depends on the probability the incumbent is the tough type.

title: Bayesian games
text:
Story
A startup founder, Eden, pitches an angel investor. Eden knows whether the startup is strong or weak. The investor can’t fully verify this in one meeting. Funding a strong startup is profitable; funding a weak one is a loss.
The investor’s action is based on beliefs about Eden’s (hidden) type.

title: Bayesian games
text:
Model

Founder type: \(\theta\in\{S,W\}\) with prior \(\Pr(S)=p\)
Investor action: fund \(F\) or reject \(R\)
Payoff to investor: if \(F\), payoff \(+1\) under \(S\) and \(-1\) under \(W\); if \(R\), payoff \(0\)

title: Bayesian games
text:
Equilibrium (threshold best response)
Investor funds iff expected payoff is nonnegative: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi \mid F]=p(1)+(1-p)(-1)=2p-1 \ge 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
p\ge \tfrac12.
\]

title: Bayesian games

Later-on analysis

Signals: if the pitch provides a signal, beliefs update via Bayes’ rule before the funding choice.
Strategic disclosure: if the founder can choose what to reveal, this becomes a signaling/cheap-talk hybrid.
Multiple types: richer type spaces yield cutoff strategies and comparative statics in \(p\).
